headline: Saturday starts a cooldown, light showers arrive Sunday into Monday, and a strong storm on an unusually southern track brings off-and-on rain, very heavy at times, from as early as Monday night through at least Wednesday morning — people near recent burn areas should prepare now.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Friday was a second straight very warm day, with highs in the upper 70s to mid 80s (Woodland Hills hit 90), 8 to 12 degrees above normal, thanks to strong high pressure and offshore (land-to-sea) winds. Skies stay clear tonight, but a broad sheet of high clouds ahead of the coming storm moves in by Saturday.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Saturday's high clouds and returning afternoon ocean breezes bring 3 to 6 degrees of cooling to most areas, including the Glendale area and the rest of the coastal valleys, though highs stay 4 to 8 degrees above normal. The coast and coastal valleys keep cooling Sunday and Monday, reaching normal or a little below, while interior areas hold steady or warm slightly this weekend and cool Monday. The first storm brings light, scattered showers to the Central Coast as early as Sunday afternoon, spreading south into Los Angeles County Sunday night into Monday morning, with under a quarter inch in most areas through Monday afternoon and up to a half inch on the Central Coast.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: The main storm could begin as early as Monday night, and models agree very well that its low pressure center will take a track much farther south than usual, a path that historically favors severe weather in Southern California, especially Los Angeles County. It will also cross ocean waters still 5 to 10 degrees warmer than normal, and many model runs have raised rain totals, especially Tuesday, when there is at least a 20 to 30 percent chance of rain falling at 1 inch per hour or more on mountain-facing slopes south of Point Conception. Forecasters urge residents, especially near areas burned in the last year or two, to start protecting property now and make evacuation plans. Thursday looks dry, and a weak system Friday will likely have little impact.

coast: A large, long-period west swell is slowly easing, but high surf continues through Saturday on the Central Coast from Point Conception northward and on the Ventura and Los Angeles County coasts, with many strong rip currents nearly everywhere, strong along-shore currents, some risk of sneaker waves, heavy shore break and beach erosion, making swimming dangerous. High Surf Advisories run until 4 PM or 9 PM Saturday depending on the stretch of coast, and a Beach Hazards Statement covers other beaches through Saturday afternoon. An exceptionally high tide of up to 7.2 feet Saturday morning keeps a threat of minor to moderate flooding in low-lying coastal spots, with a Coastal Flood Advisory for the Ventura County beaches into Saturday afternoon. On the water, a Small Craft Advisory runs until 3 AM Saturday for parts of the waters; conditions are mostly calmer Saturday through Monday evening, then winds and seas build Monday night and reach gale force Tuesday across all coastal waters, with hazardous seas, squalls with thunderstorms, possible waterspouts and poor visibility in heavy rain. Advisory-level winds and seas linger Wednesday, with a 50 percent chance of gales Wednesday night on the outer waters.
watch_for: Tuesday's heavy rain: at least a 20–30% chance of 1 inch per hour rain rates on slopes south of Point Conception, a serious concern for recent burn areas
Possible severe weather with the main storm, especially in Los Angeles County
Exact start of the main storm, possibly as early as Monday night
confidence: Forecasters are confident in the weekend cooldown and see very good model agreement on the main storm's unusually southern track, with tonight's update showing little change to the storm forecast.
